statement.title: Federal Reserve monetary policy statement, 16 September 2026
paragraphs: The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 12 – 0 vote:

The Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.
Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.

Participants anticipated upward pressure on overall inflation from high energy prices, judged employment risks tilted to the downside, and anticipated solid real GDP growth this year.

Almost all participants supported maintaining the current target range, while one participant preferred to lower it 25 basis points over concerns that the policy stance was overly restrictive amid downside labor market risks.

Almost all members agreed to maintain the target range at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent; one member voted against and preferred a 1/4 percentage point reduction, while three preferred a more two-sided characterization of future interest rate decisions.

Governor Lisa D. Cook says she felt it was appropriate not to change rates while the factors evolve and is prepared to act if she does not see signs of continued disinflation soon.

Governor Lisa D. Cook says Alaska's unemployment rate is 4.4 percent, its working-age population declined slightly in 2025, and the number of Alaskans aged 65 or older increased 3.2 percent last year.

points: Governor Christopher J. Waller says real GDP grew at a 1.8 percent annual rate in the first half of this year, while real private domestic final purchases rose 3 percent.
Governor Christopher J. Waller says job creation has increased this year by an average of 60,000 a month through July, and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent in July.
Governor Christopher J. Waller says three-month core inflation is 3.05 percent through July and has fallen steadily from 4.76 percent in February.
Governor Christopher J. Waller says he is willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level if there is continued progress toward the 2 percent goal.
Governor Christopher J. Waller says he would consider a rate hike if inflation comes in hot, and would support tighter policy if progress toward 2 percent inflation reversed in August.
Governor Christopher J. Waller says his reaction function explains how future economic data will shape his future monetary policy decisions.

fragments.text: Real GDP grew at a 1.8 percent annual rate in the first half of this year.
Overall, real private domestic final purchases, the measure of spending that best reflects the underlying strength of consumer demand, rose a strong 3 percent in the first half of 2026.
Job creation, though a bit volatile, has increased this year by an average of 60,000 a month through July.
the unemployment rate has fallen a bit to 4.1 percent in July, a historically low rate
Three-month core inflation is 3.05 percent for the three months through July, a level that is still not consistent with the FOMC's 2 percent goal.
Three-month inflation has fallen steadily from 4.76 percent in February.
If there is continued progress toward our 2 percent goal, then I am willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level.
But if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike.
If there is evidence that progress toward 2 percent inflation reversed in August, a small adjustment in our stance would help ensure that it resumes.
The second way in which I communicate is to explain how future economic data will shape my future monetary policy decisions—in short, I try to describe my "reaction function."

But if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike.
The key point here is that this it is not a commitment to a policy action—it is a conditional policy statement.

USD:speech:c2ec2c18dd9c.label: Speech
USD:speech:c2ec2c18dd9c.title: Barr, Unlocking Opportunities for Workers and Entrepreneurs with a Criminal Record
points: Governor Barr says the labor market is stable, the economy has been growing solidly, and consumer spending has been largely resilient.
Governor Barr says inflation remains too high and that he would raise rates if it appears not to be moderating sufficiently.

Governor Barr reports that the SHED found 75 percent report doing okay financially or living comfortably, while the rate is 60 percent doing at least okay financially for those convicted and once incarcerated.
Governor Barr says entrepreneurship is another path to better economic outcomes for those with a criminal record, and lending is most effective when paired with training and networks.
Governor Barr says data showing the creditworthiness of these individuals and their businesses are needed to support credit underwriting decisions.
Governor Barr says AI-powered cash flow underwriting or alternative financial data underwriting can help consumers access credit and financial products.

fragments.text: The labor market is stable, with relatively low unemployment.
The economy has been growing solidly, powered in part by the boom in AI-related business investment and the buildout of AI-related capabilities.
Consumer spending to date has been largely resilient.
But inflation remains too high—and has been for over five years.
However, if inflation appears not to be moderating sufficiently, then I think we should act decisively to raise rates.

As an example, the SHED found that, among people with no criminal records, 75 percent report doing okay financially or living comfortably, while for those convicted and once incarcerated the rate is 60 percent doing at least okay financially.
Entrepreneurship is another path to better economic outcomes for those with a criminal record.

Lending is a key input in supporting entrepreneurs with a criminal record, and it is most effective when paired with the training and networks that help a business succeed once its credit needs have been funded.
We also need data that show the creditworthiness of these individuals and their businesses to support credit underwriting decisions.
AI-powered cash flow underwriting or alternative financial data underwriting can help consumers access credit and financial products.

USD:statement:2026-04-29.label: Statement
USD:statement:2026-04-29.title: Federal Reserve monetary policy statement, 29 April 2026
points: The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3‑1/2 to 3‑3/4 percent.

The statement says recent indicators suggest economic activity has been expanding at a solid pace, job gains have remained low on average, and inflation is elevated, in part reflecting the recent increase in global energy prices.
The Committee says developments in the Middle East are contributing to a high level of uncertainty about the economic outlook, and it is attentive to risks to both sides of its dual mandate.

The Committee will carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks when considering additional target-range adjustments, and is strongly committed to supporting maximum employment and returning inflation to its 2 percent objective.
Voting for the monetary policy action were Jerome H. Powell, John C. Williams, Michael S. Barr, Michelle W. Bowman, Lisa D. Cook, Philip N. Jefferson, Anna Paulson, and Christopher J. Waller.

Stephen I. Miran preferred to lower the target range by 1/4 percentage point, while Beth M. Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie K. Logan supported maintaining the range but did not support inclusion of an easing bias.

USD:statement:2026-06-17.label: Statement
USD:statement:2026-06-17.title: Federal Reserve monetary policy statement, 17 June 2026
points: The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent.
The Committee stated that economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East.
The Committee stated that productivity growth and capital investment are strong, while job gains have kept pace with the workforce and the unemployment rate has changed little.
The Committee stated that inflation remains elevated relative to its 2 percent goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy.
The Committee reaffirmed its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.
The Federal Open Market Committee approved the statement for release by a 12 – 0 vote.

EXACT.label: EXACT
EXACT.help: Solved exactly from 1M month-average futures: the rate changes only on the effective date, so the implied rate after the meeting follows from the monthly average.

CURVE.label: CURVE
CURVE.help: OIS forward curve averaged over the interval between effective dates, minus the overnight-to-policy spread.

UPPER_BOUND.label: UPPER BOUND
UPPER_BOUND.help: 3M contract window: the average covers several meetings, so the cumulative move is an upper bound for this meeting alone.

PROXY.label: PROXY
PROXY.help: Government-curve proxy - not policy-equivalent. Shown as a raw sovereign level unless a basis can be measured from a short tenor.

DECIDED.label: DECIDED
DECIDED.help: The meeting has already been decided: it is part of the base rate.

level_help.bkbm: BKBM base: level of the ASX 90-day bank bill, not the OCR - no BKBM-OCR spread exists, so no bp vs the OCR
level_help.sovereign_proxy: sovereign proxy: raw government-curve level, not policy-equivalent

methodology.title: Base rate
methodology.text: The last rate DECIDED on or before the as-of date, including a decision that has been announced but is not in force yet (shown as 'from <date>'). The Fed is the midpoint of the target range.

methodology.title: Implied policy rate
methodology.text: Market instruments give the overnight benchmark path; the benchmark-to-policy spread (median of the last 20 business days, excluding +-2 business days around rate changes and month-ends) is removed to get a policy-equivalent rate.

methodology.title: Methods
methodology.text: EXACT: 1M month-average futures chain. CURVE: OIS forward curve averaged between effective dates. UPPER BOUND: 3M contracts whose window spans several meetings. PROXY: government curves / bills, with a basis measured only from tenors observed before the first effective date - without one ('proxy without short end') no bp, step or probability is computed and only the raw level is shown.

methodology.title: Step and probability
methodology.text: For EXACT and CURVE the implied step at the next meeting is split into whole 25 bp moves (n = floor(|step|/25)) and a fraction p of one more: P(n+1 moves) = p, P(n moves) = 1 - p, in the direction of the step.

methodology.title: Cumulative bp
methodology.text: Implied policy rate after the last meeting of the year minus the base rate, in bp. Positive = hawkish.

methodology.title: Repricing
methodology.text: Change of the implied level at a fixed horizon (last meeting of 2026 / 2027) over 5 business days (1w) and 21 business days (1m); independent of decisions taken in between. The change of the cumulative bp is a secondary field.

methodology.title: GAP
methodology.text: Market minus bank, in bp: the Fed's median dot vs the implied rate at the last meeting of each year. Only where both are on the same basis.

methodology.title: Surprises and reaction
methodology.text: Surprise vs consensus: decided rate minus consensus. Surprise vs market: decided step minus the step implied at T-1 (EXACT / CURVE / PROXY with a basis only). Reaction: change of the implied level between the close of T-1 and T at the next meeting and at the last meeting of the year.

methodology.title: Pairs
methodology.text: Base minus quote, metric by metric: the current rate differential (carry), the implied differential at year end (both legs policy-equivalent) and its repricing (both legs need a change of level). The flag is the weaker of the two legs.
